questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to challenge myself and try something completely new. I thought that if I'm traveling abroad for such a long period anyways, I might as well go to a destination further away to really make the most of it. So I chose Sydney partly due to it being very far away, but also due to it being a big hub for cultural exploration and immersion.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was certainly easier to find information after arrival than prior to it, where it often felt like navigating a jungle. We had a couple of orientation meetings with our study abroad advisor which helped a lot with information about important dates, general knowledge about the university, do's and don'ts in Australia and so on.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The orientation meetings mentioned above as well as emails summarising important information. I don't really remember everything, but I just remember getting a sense of information overload, as there was a lot of dates and stuff on top of each other to be aware of, read or complete, while at the same time recovering from jetlag and trying to find my footing in a completely new country.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: The university send out an email with names and information about different student housing providers, which definitely helped, as I could then avoid any scams by sticking to these more legit providers. They did fill up incredibly fast though, so you just had to sign up, wait and see if you'd get an offer, and then accept it within around 48-72 hours - so quite hectic. I was lucky enough to get an offer through Scape, but there are a couple of similar providers as well. I recommend trying to find accomodation as close to your university as possible, as Sydney is an incredibly big city, and travelling from one end of it to the other (like e.g. Bondi to Redfern or Newtown) can easily take an hour or more with public transport.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is incredibly expensive to live in Sydney, even if you share a room. I lived in an apartment for 8 people with 2 in each room, and even then, it cost 8000+ DKK pr. month. I was able to walk to both uni and the central business district though, so it was quite central. Though not my own experience, I heard a story from another exchange student who found housing on a third party website through direct contact with their would-be roommate. They had a horrible experience and had to move out, which also came with contractual problems, as the roommate had some administrative power due to being the primary renter and then refused to cancel the contract, so definitely be wary of stuff like that. Renting directly through a credible company, though expensive, at least gave some peace of mind by not having to worry about these things.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I honestly don't remember much from it, but they do guide you through everything you have to do via emails, though there is a lot to keep track of. There was just so much going on at the beginning, so everything is a bit of a blur.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Our study abroad advisor was a big help, as she would regularly send emails with information, reminders and just general help. She was also the one you'd usually write to with general questions about the ins and outs of the university. For help with assignments or more course-specific guidance, I found it helpful to just ask the teachers/lecturers of the given course, where I'd usually write to them through email or canvas. Some were very good at responding, others not so much, in which case I's just ask them in person at the beginning of the following class.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got accepted for all the classes I applied for (probably 7-8), after which I could choose freely between them to put together my preferred schedule (which is usually 4 courses).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember to also get pre-approval from UCPH for all courses you plan on taking (I had zero problems with this, you just have to wait a bit sometimes). Also, make sure you check course requirements through the university's "units of study" section on their website, as some classes may require that you have passed a certain amount of ECTS within that given field of study (especially relevant if you are doing electives outside of your main area of study).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses were separated into level 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000 and 5000, which corresponds with your year of study (meaning 1000 = first year/beginner, 5000 = second year postgrad level) (I believe that's how it worked, anyways). Even though I went in the third year of my bachelor, I only had level 1000 and 2000 courses, as I did electives in different subjects than my main area of study. So you don't have to only do, say, level 3000 courses if you're in your third year, you just have to make sure that you meet the prequisites for any given course (don't know if this is different for postgrad students though).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was very similar. Each course were separated into one weekly lecture and one weekly tutorial/seminar. The lectures were exactly as you'd expect, and then the tutorials were in smaller groups/classes, where you'd do some quizzes, smaller tasks, have a better chance of asking questions, and maybe delve a bit deeper into a specific subject discussed in the previous lecture of that course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: FILM1000 (Introduction to Film Studies), AMST1202 (Hashtag America: Media, Technology, Industry), MECO1001 (Introduction to Media Studies) and FILM2002 (Film Genre, Genre Film)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: This is of course very subjective, but I think that the film courses were the most interesting to me. For both courses we'd have a film screening each week, which would then be the foundation for discussing that week's topic. I really enjoyed getting to watch some great filmic masterpieces that I otherwise would have never heard about. Don't know if I'm allowed to write any names, but the two teachers/lecturers for FILM2002 in particular were some of the nicest people I've met and really made the class feel comfortable and curious about the films, so a big recommendation for that course.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Doctor's visits. I was never charged at the regular doctor's office, as I could give them my BUPA card (Overseas Student Health Coverage), which they then billed directly to them. However, having to go to any specialist, getting a blood test or basically anything else within the healthcare system was quite expensive. So even if you're able to get refunded through your own insurance afterwards, you still have to pay out of pocket in a lot of places. Just a good thing to know beforehand.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Avocados were surprisingly cheap, as I could sometimes get two very big ones for 2 AUD (around 9-10 DKK). Meat was also not too bad, but closer to danish prices. Those are the ones I remember, other things were just very expensive in general, and usually even more so than in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of different sports societies, tea clubs, film clubs, musical clubs, meet-n-greet activities and whatnot. If you can think of it, there's probably a club/society for it at the university.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Anything in the intro week that sounds interesting to you. We could book a free day trip through the university to a couple of locations in the weekend prior to the start of classes were I was able to go to the Sealife Aquarium close to Darling Harbour, so that was pretty nice. In the intro week itself, they had a bunch of different activities, most notably 2-3 days where they filled a big section of the university grounds with booths where you could hear about and join the different societies as well as get a bunch of freebies from different companies, definitely recommend to do that (you can also get multiple of the same freebies if you go on different days, just saying).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I went to New Zealand for 8 days between the end of classes and start of the exam period. Although I went in the winter and it was very cold, I would absolutely recommend that. Waitomo cave, Hobitton, Wellington and Milford Sound in particular were very beautiful locations. In Australia, I would recommend to do some day- or weekend trips to get out of the city and see either some smaller cities or the beautiful nature. I went on a surf camp to a small town 2-3 hours south of Sydney called Gerroa and also visited the neighbour town of Gerringong, both of which were stunningly beautiful. Wollongong is also an easy day trip and definitely worth a visit. For something even closer, I would absolutely recommend to go to Manly and see the main street, beach and Sydney Harbour National Park, which is only a 20-25 minute ferry ride from Circular Quay by the opera house. From there you can also take the ferry to Taronga Zoo in about 10-15 minutes and get a great view of the city from the other side of the harbour, big recommendation for that one. 
It is also possible to do a small trip to Canberra with the train ride being 4 hours each way. I personally found the capital city to quite boring as a whole, but seeing the parliament and Australian War Memorial was a pretty interesting experience. Also, if you are able, definitely try and go to the Blue Mountains as well as do either a guided tour or concert at the opera house, those are basically musts when visiting Sydney.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It wasn't too bad as Australia is culturally similar to Denmark in a lot of ways, but people are definitely a bit more open and talkative in general, which you have to get a bit used to if you're more on the introverted side.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I just tried to ask a lot of questions about the country, local culture etc., which both allowed them to talk about something familiar as well as gave me the opportunity to learn more about the culture, city and country. Often they ask back about where you come from and how your country is, and suddenly you have a conversation where you both learn something interesting about each other's culture. So I definitely recommend that strategy.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: As mentioned above, they are more open-minded than in Scandinavia, meaning you might get more questions or randomly get chatted up by a stranger. Although it can be a bit challenging, it can also make for some interesting and wholesome interactions. It also took me a while to get used to the cars driving on the left, and roundabouts in particular messed with my head before I got used to where to look.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: There were almost always a lot of things happening. There was a Diwali celebration, Chinese New Years, firework shows at Darling Harbour, Vivid Sydney and much more. So even if you are just strolling through the city, you might encounter some very interesting cultural events, light installations or similar. People in general were also pretty chill and laid-back.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Remember sunscreen (SPF 50+). The sun doesn't mess around in Australia, especially during summer. 
Also, the campus area is veeery big and (depending on your courses) you might have back-to-back  classes on opposite sites of campus, so it's a good idea to check how far you have to walk between classes. I had to leave one class a couple of minutes early each week to make it to my next class on time before they took attendance. Other than that, just any of the advice written throughout the other answers probably.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Most of the non-school stuff at university like the different societies and such are organised through/by USU (University of Sydney Union), so it's a good idea to sign up with them early, as it also allows you to get some occasional freebies and discounts. It's free to sign up, but they also have a "rewards" program for 50 AUD which for example allows you to get a free coffee each friday and additional discounts. It's probably only worth it if you do it at the start of the semester, but otherwise just getting the free membership is a good idea.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Definitely challenging myself and finding out that I am much more capable than I thought. I have always been quite scared of flying and preferred to stay in the comfort of my home country, so going to Australia for such a long time (as well as a couple of detours to New Zealand and Fiji) was the challenge of a lifetime, but it also proved to myself that I was able to do way more than I thought. I also noticed that I got a lot more comfortable over the course of my stay in terms of being far away from home, travelling on long plane rides and so on, so it definitely came with a lot of personal growth.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably being away from family and friends for so long. Because of the time difference it was e.g. a bit challenging to make calls home and it did make me feel a bit isolated sometimes. While fun at times, it could also be a bit challenging to share a room and apartment with people from all over the world, as there can be quite a big difference in what people consider to be acceptable house- and cleaning standards (at least that was the case in our apartment). But don't let this deter you from going, as it was probably just one unfortunate case among many good ones.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
If you're like me, travelling all the way to Sydney is certainly a wild ride that will challenge you in a lot of ways. But at the same time, I'm super proud to have done it and feel like I've grown a lot over the course of the stay. Just enjoy your stay as best as possible and try to be open to new experiences. Sydney is a massive city with so incredibly much to explore, discover and try, so just get out there and make some memories to last you for a lifetime (in whatever way that may be for you)!
Psst, and if you stumble upon a Yo-Chi on the way, definitely give it a try - it's really good :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
